topics.title: Projectile motion — the equation of path

questions.stem: A stone is projected from the origin at 15 m/s and 60° above the horizontal. Its motion is \(x=15t/2\) and \(y=(15\sqrt3/2)t-5t^2\). Show that its path is \(y=\sqrt3x-4x^2/45\).
questions.answer: Sample answer: From \(x=15t/2\), \(t=2x/15\). Substitute this into the vertical equation: \(y=(15\sqrt3/2)(2x/15)-5(2x/15)^2=\sqrt3x-4x^2/45\).
questions.hint: Use the horizontal equation to express t in terms of x, then substitute into the vertical equation.

keyPoints.note: Solve this equation for t before substituting.
Substitute the same t-expression into both terms.

steps.explain: Rearrange the horizontal motion equation to obtain time.

questions.stem: A stone follows the path \(y=\sqrt3x-\frac{4x^2}{45}\). What is its greatest height above the launch point?
questions.hint: The path is a downward-opening quadratic. Find its vertex or set its derivative to zero.

keyPoints.note: The maximum occurs at the vertex of the downward-opening parabola.
Differentiate with respect to x, or use the quadratic vertex formula.

steps.explain: Differentiate the height with respect to horizontal position and set the gradient to zero.

steps.explain: Substitute this x-value into the path equation.
Simplify the two terms and subtract.

questions.stem: A stone follows \(y=\sqrt3x-\frac{4x^2}{45}\) and lands on the 45° downward slope \(y=-x\). How far down the slope from the origin does it land?
questions.hint: Set the trajectory equal to the slope to find the impact x-coordinate; convert horizontal distance into distance along a 45° line.

keyPoints.note: The impact point is where the projectile path intersects this line.
A 45° slope distance is \(x/\cos45^\circ=x\sqrt{2}\), not just x.

steps.explain: Set the projectile path equal to the slope equation.
Use the nonzero intersection to get the horizontal coordinate.
Convert horizontal distance to length along the 45° slope.

questions.stem: A projectile has the path equation \(y=-3x^2+2x+4\). How far does it travel horizontally before it returns to its original height?
questions.hint: The original height is the value of y when x = 0. Set the path equation equal to that height and find the other x-intercept of the displacement from it.

keyPoints.note: The starting height is y = 4, so solve for when the path returns to y = 4.

keyPoints.text: How far does it travel horizontally
keyPoints.note: Subtract the starting horizontal position from the second solution.

steps.explain: At x=0, the projectile starts at height y=4.
Set the path equal to 4 to find when it reaches that height again.
The roots are x=0 and x=2/3. The second root is the horizontal distance from launch to the return height.

questions.stem: Zara fires a bullet horizontally from a rifle 1.70 m above level ground. Its initial horizontal speed is 360 m/s, the target is 100 m away, and gravity is 10 m/s² downward.

parts.stem: (i) Find \(\dot y\) and \(\dot x\) as functions of time.
parts.hint: Resolve the constant acceleration into horizontal and vertical components, then use the initial velocity.

keyPoints.note: Horizontal acceleration is zero; vertical acceleration is −10 m/s².
The horizontal velocity stays constant.

steps.explain: Take upward as positive. Gravity gives constant vertical acceleration −10 m/s², while horizontal acceleration is zero.

parts.stem: (ii) Find the position coordinates \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\), in metres, taking the launch point as \(x=0\).
parts.hint: Integrate each velocity component and use the launch coordinates: x=0 and y=1.70 when t=0.

keyPoints.note: Integrate the velocity components from part (i).
Use the initial conditions x(0)=0 and y(0)=1.70.

steps.explain: Integrate the constant horizontal velocity and use x(0)=0.

parts.hint: Eliminate t using x=360t, so t=x/360, and substitute into the vertical position equation.

keyPoints.note: Eliminate the time parameter from x(t) and y(t).
Substitute t=x/360 into y=−5t²+1.70.

parts.stem: (iv) How far above the ground does the bullet hit the target? Give the height to the nearest centimetre.
parts.hint: Use x=100 m in the path equation, then round the height to two decimal places because the question asks for the nearest centimetre.

keyPoints.note: The target is at horizontal distance x=100 m.
Round the height in metres to the nearest 0.01 m.

steps.explain: Substitute the target distance into the path equation.

parts.stem: (v) Find the time to reach the target and the impact speed, correct to 5 significant figures.
parts.hint: Find time from horizontal motion. At that time, combine the horizontal and vertical velocity components using Pythagoras.

keyPoints.note: Use the constant horizontal speed and the 100 m distance.
Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector, not just its horizontal component.

steps.explain: Use the horizontal motion to find the impact time.

questions.hint: Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately: horizontal velocity is constant, while gravity changes vertical velocity.

keyPoints.note: The horizontal component of velocity remains constant.
With upward positive, vertical acceleration is −10 m/s².
Use x=100 m to find the impact time and height.
